questions.question_text:
In a random sample of $600$ shoppers, $174$ used a loyalty card.
What is the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ of shoppers who used a loyalty card?

options.why: Used the $426$ shoppers who did not use a card, giving the proportion of failures instead of successes.
Gave the count $X$ rather than dividing it by $n$ to get a proportion.
Divided $n$ by $X$ instead of $X$ by $n$; a proportion can never exceed $1$.

questions.question_text:
In a large population, $28\%$ of trees are eucalypts.
A random sample of $750$ trees is taken and $\hat{p}$ is the proportion of eucalypts in the sample.
What is $E(\hat{p})$?

options.why: Gave $E(X)=np$, the expected number of eucalypts, instead of the expected proportion.
Gave $1-p$, the proportion of trees that are not eucalypts.
Divided $p$ by $n$; the division by $n$ belongs in the variance, not in the mean.
Used $np(1-p)$, which is the variance of the count $X$, not of the proportion $\hat{p}$.
Computed $p(1-p)$ but forgot to divide by $n$.
Gave the standard deviation $\sqrt{0.0004}$ instead of the variance.
Gave $\text{Var}(\hat{p})$ without taking the square root.
Computed $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$, the standard deviation of the count $X$, not of $\hat{p}$.
Took $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$ and left out the division by $n$.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(2000,0.35)$ and $\hat{p}=\dfrac{X}{2000}$.
Which pair gives $E(\hat{p})$ and $\sigma(\hat{p})$, the standard deviation correct to four decimal places?

options.why: Gave the mean and standard deviation of the count $X$ rather than of the proportion.
Took the mean of $\hat{p}$ correctly but used $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$, the spread of the count.
Took the spread of $\hat{p}$ correctly but used $E(X)=np$ as the mean.

questions.question_text:
The proportion $p$ stays the same, but the sample size is increased from $250$ to $4000$.
The standard deviation of $\hat{p}$ is multiplied by which factor?

options.why: Divided by the sample-size ratio $16$ itself instead of by its square root.
Got the size of the change right but the direction wrong; a larger sample reduces the spread.
Multiplied by the sample-size ratio, missing both the square root and the fact that the spread shrinks.

questions.question_text:
In a population, $60\%$ of members renew their subscription.
What sample size $n$ gives $\sigma(\hat{p})=0.01$ exactly?

options.why: Divided $0.24$ by $0.01$ instead of by $0.01^2$, forgetting to square the standard deviation.
Solved $\dfrac{p}{\sqrt{n}}=0.01$, using $p$ where $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$ belongs.

questions.question_text:
For a random sample of size $n$ from a binomial population, $E(\hat{p})=0.2$ and $\sigma(\hat{p})=0.02$.
What is the standard deviation of the number of successes $X$?

options.why: Stopped at $\text{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=64$ without taking the square root.
Gave $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$, the standard deviation of a single trial, instead of that of the count over $n$ trials.
Gave $\sqrt{n}=20$, an intermediate value from finding $n$, rather than the standard deviation of $X$.
